items.followUp: Why does water have a higher boiling point than ether?

rubric.why: Identifies that water molecules have stronger intermolecular attractions than alcohol molecules.
rubric.description: Water molecules form stronger hydrogen bonds with one another than alcohol molecules do.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying stronger hydrogen bonding or intermolecular forces in water than in alcohol.

rubric.why: Links stronger attractions to the energy needed to separate the molecules and hence to water’s higher boiling point.
rubric.description: More energy is needed to separate the water molecules, giving water a higher boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the stronger attractions to the greater energy requirement or higher boiling point.

modelAnswer: Water molecules form stronger hydrogen bonds with one another than alcohol molecules do.
More energy is therefore needed to separate the water molecules, giving water a higher boiling point.

items.followUp: Why does water evaporate faster when it is spread over a large surface?

rubric.why: States the effect of increasing the liquid’s exposed surface area on evaporation.
rubric.description: Increasing the surface area of a liquid increases its rate of evaporation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that evaporation becomes faster when the surface area increases.

rubric.why: Explains that a larger surface exposes more molecules that can escape into the air.
rubric.description: More molecules are exposed at the surface and can escape into the air.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that more molecules are exposed and can escape.

modelAnswer: Increasing the surface area of a liquid increases its rate of evaporation.
More molecules are exposed at the surface and can escape into the air.

items.followUp: Describe how Bohr’s model explains the line spectrum of hydrogen.

rubric.why: States Rutherford’s central nuclear structure and the atom’s mostly empty-space nature.
rubric.description: Rutherford proposed a small, dense, positively charged nucleus; most of the atom is empty space.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the positively charged nucleus or for stating that most of the atom is empty space.

rubric.why: Identifies a problem Rutherford’s theory could not explain.
rubric.description: Rutherford’s model could not explain atomic stability or line spectra.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Rutherford’s model could not explain stability, electron collapse, or line spectra.

rubric.why: Identifies Bohr’s allowed orbits or energy levels.
rubric.description: Bohr proposed that electrons can revolve only in certain fixed orbits or shells, each with a definite energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing fixed orbits, shells, or energy levels with definite energies.

rubric.why: Explains how Bohr’s allowed orbits and energy transitions address stability and account for the hydrogen line spectrum.
rubric.description: Electrons do not radiate energy in allowed orbits; they absorb or emit definite energy when jumping between levels, explaining atomic stability and the hydrogen line spectrum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons do not radiate energy in allowed orbits and 1 mark for stating that they absorb or emit definite energy during transitions, explaining the line spectrum or stability.

modelAnswer: Rutherford proposed that an atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus containing most of its mass.
Electrons revolve around the nucleus, and most of the atom is empty space.
Rutherford’s model could not explain why revolving electrons do not lose energy and fall into the nucleus, or explain atomic line spectra.
Bohr proposed that electrons can revolve only in certain fixed orbits or shells, each with a definite energy.
Electrons do not radiate energy while they remain in these allowed orbits.
An electron absorbs or emits a definite amount of energy when it jumps between energy levels; this explains atomic stability and the hydrogen line spectrum.
